2.text: Also when the son marries, and they have only a single sleeping-room, the

3.text: father cedes to the son the master’s side (aig̣ɪs˙qaoroˊn, “the left one.”)¹ If,

4.text: however, they should prefer to have separate houses, the father gives over

5.text: to the son the front house, and puts up for himself a new house in the rear.

6.text: Still I found but few facts corroborating this information. Everywhere old

7.text: men ruled, and disposed of their property; and the houses of the sons were

8.text: in the rear, not those of the fathers. When a man like Aiñanwaˊt really

9.text: does cede his house and herd to his son, it is because of personal motives,

10.text: mostly referring to the “reindeer-luck” which the old man is supposed to have

11.text: lost, while the young one hopes to acquire it again.

12.text: In the family of Eiˊheli, with his numerous sons a latent and wary

13.text: struggle against the father’s authority really took place; but the old man

14.text: jealously watched every encroachment upon his rights; and, so far as I know,

15.text: he was in full possession of them until his death, which followed a couple of

16.text: years after I left the Kolyma country.

17.text: The family or the family-group has no formal rights over the property

18.text: of its individual members. Still a man who becomes impoverished may be

19.text: reasonably sure that his nearest kinsmen will give him essential support, un-

20.text: less they are too poor or too stingy. Brother applies to brother, or cousin

21.text: to cousin, and receives a good part of the latter’s herd, so that he may be

22.text: able to start anew with his own reindeer-breeding. Thus, in the year 1894,

23.text: three brothers, sons of Taˊtko, though the eldest of them was reported to be

24.text: close-fisted, still gave to a cousin of theirs five scores² of their reindeer-does.

25.text: This cousin, in former times, also had owned a large herd, but he had squan-

26.text: dered it away. Now he was older, and expressed his intention to reform.

33.text: The chief part of the inheritance goes to the “principal heir” (eˊun-miˊlhɪlɪn).

34.text: He receives the house, and becomes the front-house master. He takes with

35.text: the house the principal ear-mark, the oldest in the herd, with which always

36.text: the greater part of the animals are maked. Other sons, and also daughters,

37.text: receive animals marked with their own ear-mark, which is assigned to them

38.text: by the father himself. When a well-to-do reindeer-breeder has no sons, and
